# Chirped Laser Pulse Control of Vibronic Wavepackets

# and Energy Transfer in Phycocyanin 645

Catrina P. Oberg1, Leah C. Spangler1,†, David F. Coker2, and Gregory D. Scholes1,*

1Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Washington Rd, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA

2Department of Chemistry, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215, USA


<!-- Page 2 -->


2

ABSTRACT: Photosynthetic organisms use light-harvesting complexes to increase the spectrum

of light that they absorb from solar photons. Recent ultrafast spectroscopic studies have revealed

that efficient (sub-ps) energy transfer is mediated by vibronic coherence in the phycobiliprotein

phycocyanin 645 (PC645).  Here, we report studies that employ broadband pump-probe

spectroscopy with linearly chirped excitation pulses to further investigate the relationship between

vibronic state preparation and energy transfer dynamics in PC645.  Negatively chirped pulse

excitation is found to enhance wavepackets of a high-frequency mode (1580 cm-1) and increase

the rate of downhill energy transfer, while on the other hand, positively chirped pulses suppress

these oscillatory features and decrease this rate. Model calculations incorporating the influence of

the chirped pump pulse are used to understand its effect on initial state preparation.  These results

provide mechanistic insight into how the overall non-equilibrium rate of energy transfer is

influenced by initial state preparation.

During photosynthesis, solar photons are captured by light-harvesting antenna complexes and

the excitation energy is funneled to the reaction center where charge separation occurs.1–6  An

evolutionary design of down conversion in light-harvesting proteins allows for a broad wavelength

range of light to be absorbed by the antenna.3–5,7  Cryptophyte algae use light harvesting antenna

called phycobiliproteins (PBPs), which contain a series of bilin chromophores to harvest light in

the center of the visible spectrum and down convert the absorbed energy to the chlorophyll-

containing complexes with near-unit quantum efficiency.8–11   This initial stage of energy transfer

has a remarkably high efficiency and occurs on the femtosecond to picosecond timescale,1,10–16

motivating the need for femtosecond spectroscopy. Recent ultrafast spectroscopic studies have

generated interest in the role that vibrational and electronic coherence play during energy

transfer.17–20  Coherent oscillations observed in PBPs are attributed to vibrational and electronic

coherence with dephasing times on a sub-ps timescale, the same timescale as the fastest energy

transfer step.1,10,14,15,21–23 In addition to cryptophyte algae, coherence has since been detected in

many photosynthetic systems, including purple bacteria24–26, green sulfur bacteria27,28,

cyanobacteria29,30, and dinoflagellates31–33.

Light-harvesting dynamics are often studied using femtosecond laser experiments based on

ultrafast broadband pulses. Relevant experiments include broadband pump probe (BBPP) and two-

dimensional electronic spectroscopy (2DES). Unlike narrowband excitation, these pulses

coherently excite both the donor and acceptor, and it has not been well explored how broadband

pulse excitation might affect measurements of the ultrafast dynamics. In this work, we study the

effects of coherent initial state preparation on energy transfer in a PBP isolated from Chroomonas

mesostigmatica cryptophyte algae, a light-harvesting complex known as phycocyanin 645

(PC645).

PC645 is a closed-form (αβ)2 homodimer that binds eight chromophores: two central

dihydrobiliverdins (DBVs), two mesobiliverdins (MBVs), and four peripheral phycocyanobilins

(PCBs).  Stick spectra in Fig. 1A show the estimated absorbances of the DBV, MBV, and PCB

bilins that contribute to the linear absorbance spectrum.12  The positions of the bilins in the crystal

structure34 are shown in Fig. 1B along with the reported energy transfer pathways (with time

constants, in picoseconds) from narrowband transient absorption experiments.13  The DBVs (blue)

are found as a central dimer that are strongly coupled (320 cm-1) to form a delocalized molecular

exciton pair (DBV– and DBV+) and make up the 585 nm absorbance band.1  The lower-energy


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

PCBs (red) make up the 645 nm band, and the two MBVs (green) absorb around 620 nm.  The

fastest downhill energy transfer step occurs within approximately 600 fs from the higher-energy

donor DBVs to the lower-energy acceptor PCBs (Fig. 1B, yellow arrows), spanning an energy gap

of 1580 cm-1.13 This efficient (sub-ps) energy transfer cannot be described by Förster theory alone

and, instead, is explained by a combination of spectral overlap and vibronic (mixed vibrational-

electronic) coupling.10 The 1585 cm-1 mode, which oscillates at a frequency that matches the DBV–

PCB energy gap and has vibronic character, is proposed to mediate sub-ps energy transfer in

PC645.

To examine the impact of vibronic character on energy transfer, we use broadband pump-probe

spectroscopy with linearly chirped excitation pulses to simultaneously study energy transfer and

coherence dynamics.  In this technique, a spectrally broad excitation pulse with a shorter time

duration than the vibrational period projects population from the ground state to the excited state

and impulsively generates a wavepacket, a superposition of quantum states that periodically

modulates the BBPP amplitude as it evolves in time.35–41  These wavepackets provide a way to

pinpoint the involvement of particular vibrational degrees of freedom in excited state dynamics.42

Optical control of ultrafast processes has been demonstrated through pulse shaping to enhance

the rate of two-photon absorption,43 increase the yield of photoinduced electron transfer,44 and

enhance specific vibrational modes in a crystal lattice.45  However these experiments require the

use of additional instrumentation (such as spatial light modulators) and feedback loops.  Instead,

linearly chirped laser pulses, where the frequency of the pulse changes linearly with time over the

pulse envelope, can be used to control the vibrational wavepacket amplitude without a pulse shaper

or additional optics. Negatively chirped pulses have the higher-energy wavelengths arrive at the

sample before the lower-energy side, while positively chirped pulses are temporally ordered from


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

low to high energy.  Such chirped laser pulses have been shown to manipulate wavepacket

dynamics,46,47 optimize population transfer,48,49 characterize solvent environment,50 and

theoretically control vibronic state preparation.51  Particularly, the chirp (or slope) of the pulse

frequency as a function of time has been found to favor (negative chirp) or disfavor (positive chirp)

the formation of vibrationally-hot ground state wavepackets.51 However, chirped pump pulses have

not been used to study the relationship between coherent wavepackets, vibrational populations,

and energy transfer in photosynthetic systems.  Here we use linearly chirped broadband excitation

pulses to control the initial vibronic state preparation of PC645 and probe the link between energy

transfer and vibrational dynamics.

and represents the pulse of shortest time duration for a given pulse spectrum. The compression

was adjusted to produce two linearly chirped pulses – a negatively chirped pulse (NC) and a

positively chirped pulse (PC) – with the same frequency distribution (Fig. 1A, yellow) and

The transient absorption (TA) spectrum for excitation of PC645 using the TL pump pulse is

shown in Fig. 2A.  The broad, positive region (550-675 nm) is a combination of the ground state

bleaching (GSB) and stimulated emission (SE) features and will be discussed in detail.  The red-

shifted negative feature is commonly called an excited state absorption due to the opposite sign

relative to the bleach, but is likely due to the inertial response of an impulsively driven oscillator52

as well as scatter from the protein. Therefore, this feature will not be used to assign coherences. In

*Fig. 2B, kinetic traces at two representative probe wavelengths show that energy is transferred*

acceptor.  The broadband excitation pulse also produces coherent wavepackets, which are

To isolate the coherence data from the population dynamics, the population kinetics are fit and

then subtracted to leave the residual data (Fig. S2B) containing only the oscillatory dynamics. The


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

residual data are Fourier transformed to produce a power spectrum depicting a 2D map of the

coherences as a function of probe wavelength, shown in Fig. 2C.  The power spectrum for TL

excitation shows numerous, well-resolved vibronic features up to 1800 cm-1, with most of the

features in the low frequency regime below 1000 cm-1. The largest amplitudes are observed at

probe wavelengths between 630-670 nm, which is where the PCBs absorb.

Summation across all probe wavelengths of the power spectrum in Fig. 2C produces an

integrated coherence map (Fig. 3A, black).  For clarity, Fig. 3A compares the integrated plots for

the three excitation pulses (TL, NC, and PC).  The integrated coherence plots reveal that there is

chirp-dependence on the overall amplitude of the oscillatory features.  In particular, TL and NC

are well-resolved while PC shows significant damping especially in the region of higher

frequencies above about 800 cm-1.  Relative to TL excitation, NC coherence plots have three modes

with increased intensity: 985 cm-1, 1325 cm-1, and 1580 cm-1.  In comparison, PC excitation

resolves a few low-frequency vibrations, but the high-frequency modes (including the 1580 cm-1

mode) are noticeably damped.  Since wavepackets comprising the mode at 1580 cm-1 exhibit the

most significant chirp-dependent properties, we focus our discussion on this feature.

The primary amplitude of the coherent oscillations is in the 650 nm region, corresponding to the

bleach region where the PCB acceptor bilins absorb light.  The 1580 cm-1 mode is assigned to C=N

stretching of the bilins and, interestingly, its frequency closely matches the energy gap between

DBV donors and PCB acceptors.10,53 The chirp-dependent behavior of this mode can be

rationalized using the mechanism of wavepacket formation, shown in Fig. 3B.46–48 With a

negatively chirped pulse, the first field-matter interaction of the pump creates a coherence on the

electronic excited state. The non-equilibrium vibronic wavepacket begins to move over the excited

state potential energy surface before a second field-matter interaction with the lower energy side


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

of the negatively chirped pump projects the wavepacket back down to the ground electronic state,

but now with higher vibrational energy. Therefore, a negatively chirped pulse favors the formation

of a ground-state wavepacket.  Since the probe integrated power spectrum feature at 1580 cm-1 is

enhanced by negative chirped excitation, we can primarily assign it to an impulsively excited

ground state wavepacket in this mode of the PCB bilins. Furthermore, the FT coherence map (Fig.

2C) may be showing a progression along the 1580 cm-1 feature, which supports an assignment to

ground state coherences. The positively chirped pulse is ordered from low to high frequency, so

the two field interactions produce more overall amplitude in the excited electronic state vibronic

wavepacket, suppressing the formation of the 1580 cm-1 vibrational mode on the ground electronic

state. Detailed vibronic wavepacket dynamics simulations of this behavior are presented in the SI.

To further analyze the origin of these coherence changes, we examine the data in a region where

PCB bilins absorb, corresponding to the PCB ground state wavepacket.  The kinetic traces for the

three excitation conditions centered at 655 nm are shown in Fig. 4A.  In the first picosecond, strong

oscillatory features are observed for TL and NC excitation conditions.  However, the amplitude of

oscillations produced by PC excitation (orange) is noticeably reduced.  Taking a Fourier transform

of the oscillations (Fig. 4B) reveals the suppression of high frequency oscillations as well as low

frequency oscillations for the PC excitation case at this probe wavelength, while TL and NC

coherence features are well-resolved past 1600 cm-1.  These observations match the trends in Fig.

3A, showing that excitation with the positively chirped pulse reduces the amplitude of wavepacket

oscillations of the PCB bilin vibrations.  These observations support the conclusion that negative

chirp favors the formation of ground state wavepackets on the PCB acceptor while positive chirp

suppresses this ground state wavepacket.

The results in this report imply that the chirped pulse excitation affects state preparation in

PC645, with the enhancement (suppression) of a vibrational mode resonant with the donor-

acceptor energy gap using negatively chirped (positively chirped) pump pulses.  Therefore, we

hypothesize that if vibronic coherence does affect the energy transfer rate, we should see different

population dynamics as a function of pulse chirp. While factors other than pulse chirp affect the

transient absorption signal, including the vibrational frequency and time duration of the pump

pulse,54,55 these factors were controlled in the design of the experiments, detailed in SI. To uncover

the role of the 1580 cm-1 mode in energy transfer, the population dynamics and mechanism of chirp

dependence are explored.

In photosynthetic systems like PC645, the population data reveal information about how energy

is transferred through the protein.  However, the time constants of energy transfer between

individual chromophores cannot be traced in broadband experiments.  Instead, downhill energy

transfer is observed, and the ensemble data are fit with exponential decays/growths.

To quantify the energy transfer kinetics, the data were fit with four parallel lifetimes by

performing global analysis using Glotaran56 for each excitation pulse data set.  This fit is depicted

as decay-associated difference spectra (DADS) in Fig. 4C for the TL excitation pulse and Fig. S3

of the SI for the chirped pulses.  The overall line shapes show the same characteristics as TL

excitation, where the positive amplitudes of the DADS represent exponential decay while the

negative amplitudes represent exponential growth for the GSB/SE region (560 nm-675 nm).  We

focus the analysis on the fastest event (τ1), which was fit with the black DADS trace with a sub-

ps lifetime, since it is relevant to donor to acceptor EET.  An analysis of the other DADS fits is

found in the SI.  Within τ1, there is a simultaneous exponential decay (550-600 nm) and growth

(630-675 nm) with a derivative-like shape that indicates energy transfer from the higher energy


<!-- Page 13 -->


13

DBVs to lower energy PCB acceptors.  The lifetime of the fastest energy transfer event (~450 fs)

is on the same timescale as previously reported fitting for broadband excitation of PC645.15,16

We now address the most significant findings of our work. While the overall DADS line shapes

did not change as a function of chirp, the τ1 time constant showed chirp-dependence (Table 1).

The τ1 time constant is approximately 25 fs (6%) faster under negatively chirped excitation relative

to the TL excitation.  However, the τ1 of the positively chirped pulse excitation is longer than the

TL excitation case by approximately 10% (40 fs).

To gain a mechanistic understanding of these experimental results, we detail a simple model in

the SI of how a chirped pump pulse can influence the preparation of different vibronic state

superposition wavepackets depending on the pulse characteristics including pulse duration, linear

chirp, frequency distribution, detuning relative to the molecular transition energies, and strength

of the pump field – matter interaction.

Several previous theoretical studies have explored the influence of chirped laser pulses on

processes like population transfer and selective vibronic excitation.57–62 Our simulations solve the

field driven time–dependent Schrödinger equation for the time–dependent amplitudes of the

different vibronic states of our model as the shaped pulse passes through the system.  This model


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

includes electronic ground and excited state harmonic potential surfaces that are displaced relative

to one another along a normal mode coordinate with frequency 1600 cm-1, mimicking the

excitation of the chromophores in the PC645 system.  Here, we analyze the results of simulations

using this model to provide a detailed understanding of the experimental observations on the

influence of chirp on initial state preparation and subsequent energy transfer kinetics.

The first characteristic of note from Fig. S5 is that the asymptotic population of the initially

populated unexcited ground vibrational state, G(0), is insensitive to the sign of the chirp. The

detailed Rabi cycling dynamics of the population of this state during the positive and negative

chirped pulses is clearly different, with, for example, the positive chirped pump pulse for this

detuning coming into resonance with transitions out of this ground state earlier in the pulse than

with the negative chirped pump. After the pump has passed, the asymptotic G(0) state population

prepared by the pump is independent of the sign of the chirp; this insensitivity to the sign of the

chirp is explored in the SI.

However, the branching to other vibrational and vibronic levels is significantly and selectively

dependent on the sign of the chirp, as demonstrated by the results presented on an expanded scale

in Fig. 4D.  Here, examples of the following general trends, detailed in the SI, are observed: (1)

the population in the lowest vibronic level on the excited electronic state, E(0), is significantly

enhanced by positive chirp and suppressed by negative chirp (solid orange and blue curves,

respectively); (2) the population of the first excited vibronic level on the excited electronic state,

E(1), shows the opposite trend, being suppressed by the positive chirp and enhanced by the

negative chirp (dashed orange and blue curves, respectively); and (3) at later times during the pump

pulse, population is projected to the vibrationally excited ground electronic state G(1).  This

process is strongly suppressed with positive chip and enhanced with negative chirp (dotted orange


<!-- Page 15 -->


15

and blue curves, respectively). While this G(1) population is only a few percent for the simulation

results reported in Fig. 4D, the magnitude of the asymptotic G(1) population can be influenced by

pulse duration and detuning as outlined in the SI. A final general trend to note is that the asymptotic

populations produced by pumping with the equivalent transform limited pulse, not surprisingly,

always lie in between those resulting from pumping with the positive and negative chirped pulses.

The general observation that the positive chirp strongly suppresses the population of the G(1) state

provides a clear mechanism for the experimentally observed suppression of the ground state

vibrational wavepacket with positive chirp as reported in Figs. 3(A), and 4(A) and (B).

When planning this study, we had intuitively thought that enhancing the wavepacket amplitude

would enhance the vibronic mechanism for EET. After more careful analysis, the interpretation of

the results is more complicated. Furthermore, our findings are of more general interest because

they show how the dynamics measured by broadband femtosecond experiments, like two-

dimensional electronic spectroscopy, are influenced by non-equilibrium initial state preparation.

Here we explain our experimental results using two facts. First, when an acceptor chromophore

(PCB) is photo-excited, it does not quench the donor (DBV) excited state by an EET mechanism.

Indeed, if the PCB chromophore is sufficiently highly excited, for example to its E(1) state which

is close to resonant with the DBV E(0) initially excited donor state, delocalization between these

chromophores can enhance the amplitude of the initial state of the EET process. Second, in PC645,

an initially excited DBV donor can be quenched by EET to one of four possible un-excited PCB

acceptors, and the measured EET rate, or time constant, is the overall net rate of donor quenching

by the various available acceptors. Since the PCB E(1) state is close to resonant with the initial

DBV E(0) donor “reactant” state, the lower energy terminal “product” state of the EET process is

the PCB E(0) state. Therefore, we propose that if, for example, one of the PCB acceptors is


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

electronically excited to its PCB E(0) state during initial state preparation, one pathway to this

EET product state is blocked.  In this scenario, the remaining three un-excited ground-state PCB

chromophores can serve as acceptors of excitation energy from the donor state, but the net EET

rate constant must be slower since one quenching pathway is now blocked due to the excitation of

one of the possible product states. On this basis, we can rationalize the observation of the influence

of chirp on the measured net EET rate constant by considering how chirp-pulse excitation affects

the PCB excited state production by the mechanism of enhancing or suppressing excitation of

different vibronic excited state levels on the acceptor. As outlined above, the simulation results

presented in the SI show the general trend of suppressing the initially prepared E(0) EET acceptor

product state population with negative chirp and enhancing it with positive chirp.

This negative chirp product state suppression of the PCB E(0) can arise from two possible

pathways:(i) preparation of increased population in the PCB E(1) state (reducing PCB E(0)), which

can delocalize to the near degenerate DBV donor E(0) reactant state, increasing the EET reactant

population and consequently the forward rate, or (ii) projection of amplitude from the PCB E(0)

product state back down to its G(1) state driven by the later arriving lower energy tail of the

negative chirp pump pulse. Negative chirp suppression of the initial product state (relative

enhancement of the reactant state) increases the forward rate, while the opposite influences of

positive chirp (increasing the initial EET product state and reducing the reactant state) must slow

the forward EET rate. Hence, negative chirp excitation minimizes blocking of the EET, increasing

the measured net rate of EET. On the other hand, positive chirp excitation enhances the population

of the PCB E(0) product state, increasing the reverse rate, and thereby effectively blocking an EET

pathway and reducing the measured net rate of EET.

The results of the global analysis fitting displayed in Figs. S3 and S4, with time constants

summarized in Table S2, suggest that, in addition to τ1~450 fs EET process, which speeds up

with negative chirp, there is a slower component EET process with τ2~1.5 ps, which, in contrast,

shows an apparent slowing with negative chirp. While the DADS curves suggest that the initial

state for τ1 is localized in energy on a state at near 585 nm, τ2 displays delocalization in energy

over the higher energy state and a lower energy donor (630 nm) state. As indicated by our

simulation results, NC produces a relative suppression of the acceptor E(0) product state

resulting in a net increase in the fast component of the EET rate to this state due to multiple

acceptor pathways being open with this initialization. At the same time, NC enhances the

production of the acceptor vibronic exited state E(1), which is close to resonant with the lower

part of the band of donor states close to the 630 nm region. States in this energy range are thus

expected to be spatially delocalized between the donor and acceptor molecules, and the spatial

delocalization in this excited vibronic state will generally result in slower vibrational relaxation

to the final EET product state, PCB E(0). Negative chirp (larger acceptor E(1) amplitude) results

in stronger delocalization between the two chromophores, further slowing the vibronic relaxation

rate component consistent with the observed chirp dependence of the slower τ2 relaxation time.

Although algae use incoherent light as a source for photosynthesis63, ultrafast laser experiments

do not mimic natural excitation conditions. Prior work64 has established that cryptophyte algae

species undergo photoacclimation in response to different spectral filtering conditions of

incoherent light. However, under coherent excitation, vibronic coupling for EET suggests that

there is an enhancement of spectral overlap by a vibrational resonance with a frequency of 1580

cm-1.10 We can therefore use ultrafast coherent laser spectroscopy as a tool to reveal the underlying

energy transfer steps and mechanism that are usually hidden, and we provide further evidence that


<!-- Page 18 -->


18

vibronic coupling is involved in efficient EET. By selectively enhancing or suppressing the

resonant vibronic mode (1580 cm-1) between the donor and acceptor using chirped pulses, we

uncover how the broadband pulse affects the energy transfer rate coefficient. The mechanism of

this chirp dependence was investigated using simulations of the interaction of the time dependent

pump field with a multi-state vibronic model of the chromophores, which supported the

supposition that initial state preparation affects the amplitudes of the different component vibronic

states that comprise the initially exited wavepacket. We find that positively chirped pulses

enhanced initial excitation of the PCB acceptor and slowed the measured energy transfer rate by

approximately 10% compared to experiments with transform limited excitation. We propose that

this enhanced population of excited PCB acceptor state produced by the positively chirped pulse

decreases the net EET rate by blocking one of the four acceptor sites in the complex.
